**Proof.**

By hypothesis $X_n \to +\infty$ almost surely, i.e. there exists an event $\Omega_0$ with $P(\Omega_0)=1$ such that for every $\omega\in\Omega_0$,
$$X_n(\omega)\to +\infty \quad\text{as } n\to\infty.$$

Recall that $X_n(\omega)\to+\infty$ means: for every real threshold $K$, there exists an integer $N=N(\omega,K)$ such that for all $n\ge N$, $X_n(\omega)>K$.

Fix an arbitrary $M>0$. We must show $P(X_n<M \text{ i.o.})=0$, where
$$\{X_n<M \text{ i.o.}\}=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\{X_n<M\}=\bigcap_{N=1}^{\infty}\bigcup_{n\ge N}\{X_n<M\}.$$

Take any $\omega\in\Omega_0$. Applying the definition of $X_n(\omega)\to+\infty$ with the threshold $K=M$, there exists $N_0=N(\omega,M)$ such that for all $n\ge N_0$,
$$X_n(\omega)>M,$$
equivalently $\omega\notin\{X_n<M\}$ for every $n\ge N_0$. Hence $\omega$ belongs to only finitely many of the events $\{X_n<M\}$, so
$$\omega\notin\{X_n<M \text{ i.o.}\}.$$

Since this holds for every $\omega\in\Omega_0$, we obtain
$$\{X_n<M \text{ i.o.}\}\subseteq \Omega_0^{c}.$$

Therefore
$$P(X_n<M \text{ i.o.})\le P(\Omega_0^{c})=1-P(\Omega_0)=0.$$

Being a probability, $P(X_n<M \text{ i.o.})\ge 0$, so
$$P(X_n<M \text{ i.o.})=0.$$

Since $M>0$ was arbitrary, the claim holds for every $M>0$. $\blacksquare$
